docs.text: ESP32 Devices & Modules Documentation ¶ Welcome to the documentation for custom ESP32-based smart home devices and firmware modules. This documentation provides setup guides, hardware specifications, and detailed MQTT API references for integrating devices with Home Assistant and other smart home platforms. Main Sections ¶ How-to Guides : Step-by-step instructions for initial setup, Wi-Fi configuration, factory reset, and firmware updates. Devices : Hardware specifications, power requirements, and module listings for all supported hardware models (Audio Player, Button Box). Settings : Device configuration settings (work in progress). Modules : Firmware modular components with detailed MQTT commands, status payloads, and telemetry specifications. Versioning & URL Access ¶ This documentation is deployed to GitHub Pages under a versioned path ( .../v1/... ). Major MQTT API revisions will introduce newer version paths.

docs.text: Audio Player v0 ¶ The Audio Player v0 is an ESP32-based network audio player featuring an onboard temperature/humidity sensor and multi-color RGB LED status feedback. Hardware Specification ¶ Power Input: 12V DC, center positive. Recommended power supply: 2A . Fuse: 1.35A or 1.5A 5x20mm glass fuse. Buttons: 1 physical button (for AP mode, factory reset, and custom actions). Included Modules ¶ This device includes the following hardware and software modules: SHT40 (temperature & humidity sensor) Button Audio (WAV player with 10 sinks) RGB LED Time (network time synchronization) WiFi (wireless networking) MQTT (telemetry and command interface) Factory reset (factory restore handling) Settings (configuration management) File storage (onboard flash storage) General (system telemetry and status supervisor)

docs.text: Factory Reset ¶ Performing a factory reset deletes all stored Wi-Fi credentials and configurations, restoring the device to its default factory state. Manual Factory Reset (Hardware Button) ¶ When the device cannot be reached over the network: Unplug the power supply from the device. Press and hold down the hardware button (on the Button Box, press the button at Row 1, Column 1). Plug the power supply back in while continuously holding down the button. Wait for more than 10 seconds ( >10s ). Release the button. The device will reset to factory defaults and restart in AP mode. Software Factory Reset (Web Interface) ¶ When the device is accessible on the local network: Open the device web interface in your browser: http://<DEVICE_IP> Navigate to the Factory reset menu option. Confirm the reset. The device will clear its settings and reboot.

docs.text: Firmware Update ¶ The device firmware can be easily updated over the local network through its built-in web portal by uploading a new binary ( .bin ) file. Update Procedure ¶ Open the device web portal in your browser: http://<DEVICE_IP> Select the Firmware update menu item. Select and upload the provided firmware binary ( .bin format). Wait for the upload and flashing process to complete. Once flashing completes, the device will automatically reboot running the new firmware.

docs.text: Quick Start Guide ¶ Essential steps to get your device powered on, connected to your local Wi-Fi network, and operational. 1. Connect to the Configuration Access Point ¶ Power on the device. Using a smartphone or laptop, search for Wi-Fi networks and connect to the access point named ESP32_AP_... . Open a web browser to access the configuration portal (or wait for the captive portal prompt). 2. Configure Wi-Fi Credentials ¶ Enter your local Wi-Fi SSID and password . Click Save . After saving, the device will automatically reboot and attempt to connect to the configured network. Static IP Recommendation It is highly recommended to assign a static IP reservation in your router for the device MAC address to ensure consistent network addressing and reliable home automation integration. 3. Unsuccessful Connection: Forcing AP Mode ¶ If the device fails to connect to the Wi-Fi network or credentials change, you can force it back into Access Point (AP) mode: Unplug the power supply from the device. Press and hold down the hardware button (on the Button Box, press the button at Row 1, Column 1). Plug the power supply back in while holding the button. Wait 2 seconds , then release the button. The device will start in AP mode ( ESP32_AP_... ).

docs.text: Modules Overview ¶ The ESP32 firmware features a modular architecture: every smart device model is composed from a combination of these specialized hardware and software components. Each module manages a focused domain and interacts over a unified MQTT interface. Available Modules ¶ General : System supervisor, telemetry aggregation, reset reason monitoring, and software reboot triggers. Audio : Multi-channel (10 sinks) WAV playback from internal flash or remote HTTP streaming with priority handling and prebuffering. File storage : Internal flash memory filesystem management (8MB), remote HTTP upload, file deletion, and directory listing over MQTT. MQTT : Broker connection management, SSL/TLS security, unique and common group subscriptions, and connection error metrics. RGB LED : Addressable Neopixel LED driver with color/brightness controls and automatic offline network status alerts. Settings : Built-in asynchronous HTTP webserver for browser-based module and hardware configuration. SHT40 : Sensirion digital temperature and relative humidity measurements with telemetry error tracking. Time : Network NTP synchronization, POSIX timezone support, and Unix timestamp publishing. WiFi : AP setup mode, STA client networking, and boot-time strongest signal mesh connection locking. Button : Momentary pushbutton driver with single-click, double-click, and long-press event detection. Button matrix : Multiplexed keypad driver (e.g. 16-key console) with a dedicated hardware reboot trigger. Rotary encoder : Quadrature knob decoder with batch rotation tracking and relative delta reporting. RYG status LED : Discrete Red, Yellow, and Green visual status indicators for Wi-Fi, MQTT, and telemetry pulses. Factory reset : Complete non-volatile memory wipe, default restoration, and monochrome LED blink pattern progress feedback.

docs.text: Audio Module ¶ The Audio module provides playback capabilities for WAV audio streams and files on the device (via I2S DAC / amplifier). Key Features ¶ Supported Audio Format: Currently, only WAV format is supported, with standard 44-byte PCM headers . 10 Independent Audio Sinks (0–9): Each sink has an independently configurable volume ( 0 – 100 ). Priority Interruption: Playback on a lower-indexed sink interrupts any active playback on higher-indexed sinks (e.g., sink 0 preempts sinks 1–9). Playback Sources: Flash Storage: Playback from internal flash storage (typical capacity is 8MB; requires the File storage module ). Network URL (HTTP Stream): Direct streaming and playback from a local or remote HTTP URL. Buffering & Prebuffer: Playback utilizes dedicated memory buffering (typically 4MB PSRAM). Audio output only begins once the buffer fills to a pre-configured threshold (prebuffer size). This threshold can be configured separately in settings for network streams and local files. Scheduled Playback: Playback can be scheduled to begin at a specific future timestamp using the startAt parameter. This must fall between current device time and now + 15 seconds (in epoch milliseconds). Volume Adjustment Notice Frequent adjustments and writes to sink volume levels are not recommended due to limited flash write cycles (premature flash memory wear). MQTT Interface ¶ Subscriptions (Commands) ¶ Unique and Common Topic Support All command topics listed below subscribe to both the device-specific base topic ( <topic>/command/... ) and the configurable shared common topic ( <common_topic>/command/... ). This allows simultaneous playback, group stopping, or mass volume changes across multiple audio player nodes at once. 1. Stop Playback ¶ Topic: <topic>/command/audio Payload: raw string: stop 2. Play Local File ¶ Topic: <topic>/command/playFile JSON Fields: path (string, required): File path in flash storage (e.g. "/doorbell.wav" ). sink (number, required): Target sink index ( 0 – 9 ). startAt (number, optional): Playback start timestamp in epoch millis ( now to now + 15s ). Example immediate playback: {"path": "/doorbell.wav", "sink": 0} Example scheduled playback: {"path": "/doorbell.wav", "sink": 0, "startAt": 1791922925635} 3. Play Remote URL Stream ¶ Topic: <topic>/command/playHost JSON Fields: url (string, required): HTTP URL of the audio stream/file on LAN or internet. sink (number, required): Target sink index ( 0 – 9 ). startAt (number, optional): Playback start timestamp in epoch millis ( now to now + 15s ). Example immediate stream: {"url": "http://192.168.1.100/doorbell.wav", "sink": 0} Example scheduled stream: {"url": "http://192.168.1.100/doorbell.wav", "sink": 0, "startAt": 1791922925635} 4. Set Volume ¶ Topic: <topic>/command/volume/<sink> sink : Target sink index ( 0 – 9 ) Payload: Volume integer between 0 and 100 . Publications ¶ State Changes (Status) ¶ Topic: <topic>/status Published on playback state transitions: audio.volume : Array of 10 integers representing volumes of sinks 0–9 ( 0 – 100 ). audio.playState : Player engine state REQUEST_START STARTING PREBUFFER WAITING RUNNING REQUEST_STOP STOPPING STOPPED UNKNOWN audio.downloadState : Stream downloader / file reader state: REQUEST_START STARTING RUNNING REQUEST_STOP STOPPING STOPPED UNKNOWN audio.bufferUsed : Current buffer memory utilization in bytes ( 0 to 4MB , depends on hardware). Example Payload: { "audio": { "volume": [5, 5, 18, 5, 5, 3, 5, 5, 5, 1], "playState": "RUNNING", "downloadState": "STOPPED", "bufferUsed": 2715820 } } Telemetry ¶ Topic: <topic>/telemetry audio_buf_errors : Number of critical buffer read/underrun errors that caused playback to abort. Example Payload: { "audio_buf_errors": 0 } Settings ¶ Configurable buffering parameters in the web portal: File start buffer (bytes): Playback begins after reading and filling the buffer with this amount of data when playing local WAV files from flash storage. Recommended value: 16 kB (16384 bytes). Network start buffer (bytes): Playback begins after downloading and filling the buffer with this amount of data when streaming from a remote HTTP URL. Recommended value: 16–256 kB (depending on Wi-Fi channel noise and latency). Increase this value if audio playback starts with stuttering or initial pops.

docs.text: Button Matrix Module ¶ The Button matrix module scans and manages multiplexed pushbutton arrays (such as the 4x4 matrix on the Button Box v1). Operating Behavior ¶ Supported Gesture: Matrix buttons support single push detection only. Special Hardware Reboot Button (Row 3, Column 3): The key at coordinates (3, 3) (Row 4, Column 4 with 0-based indexing) functions as a dedicated physical reset trigger. Pressing this button sends no MQTT messages and immediately reboots the device . MQTT Interface ¶ Publications ¶ When a standard matrix key is pressed, an event is published: Topic: <topic>/button_<row>_<column> <row> : Row index ( 0 -based: 0, 1, 2, 3). <column> : Column index ( 0 -based: 0, 1, 2, 3). Payload: ON : The button was pressed. Example Payload for button at Row 0, Column 1: Topic: <topic>/button_0_1 Payload: ON

docs.text: Button Module ¶ The Button module handles debouncing, gesture recognition, and event publishing for directly connected physical momentary pushbuttons. Supported Gestures ¶ The module recognizes three distinct user interaction gestures: Single Click ( click ): A standard, short press. Double Click ( doubleClick ): Two consecutive presses in rapid succession. Long Press ( longPressStart ): Continuous press held beyond the long-press threshold duration. MQTT Interface ¶ Publications ¶ When a button gesture is detected, the event is immediately published: Topic: <topic>/status/button_<index> <index> : Button index (starting from 0 ). Payload Options: click doubleClick longPressStart Example Payload for single click on button 0: Topic: <topic>/status/button_0 Payload: click

docs.text: Factory Reset Module ¶ The Factory reset module handles clearing stored configurations and restoring default firmware factory settings. Operating Behavior & Scope ¶ What is Cleared: Factory reset wipes all stored settings (Wi-Fi credentials, MQTT parameters, custom configurations) and deletes all user-uploaded files stored in flash memory. What is Preserved: Previously installed firmware updates are preserved (the device remains on its currently installed firmware binary rather than reverting to ancient factory flashing). Execution Methods ¶ Factory reset can be triggered via two paths: 1. Hardware Button: Powering on the device while holding the setup button for >10 seconds . 2. Software Web UI: Using the Factory reset option in the web configuration portal. For step-by-step procedures, refer to the Factory Reset Guide . LED Blink Sequence during Hardware Reset ¶ During a hardware button reset—while reconnecting power and continuously holding the button—an onboard monochrome indicator LED signals the progress: Flashes once per second for 0.1 seconds . Then flashes 5 times (0.1 seconds ON) every 100 ms . Finally turns solid ON for 1 second . At this point, the factory reset is complete, and the button can be released. Absence of RGB LED Indication The addressable RGB LED module will not light up or provide feedback during factory reset, because complex peripheral drivers are not yet initialized during early boot execution. Reconfiguration ¶ After a factory reset completes, the device restarts in AP mode. To configure the device again, follow the Quick Start Guide .

docs.text: File Storage Module ¶ The File storage module manages the onboard non-volatile SPIFFS/LittleFS flash filesystem. It allows storing audio files (e.g. doorbells, ringtones, alerts), downloading files remotely over HTTP, deleting files, and querying the file index via MQTT. Operating Behavior ¶ Storage Capacity: Flash storage space is limited (typically 8MB , depending on the hardware partition table). Safe Upload Check: If an incoming download exceeds available free flash storage space, the module immediately aborts the download and prevents storage overflow. Common Topic Support: In addition to the unique <topic>/command/fs , the module subscribes to the configurable common base topic ( <common_topic>/command/fs ), allowing one command to upload or manage files across multiple nodes simultaneously. MQTT Interface ¶ Subscriptions (Commands) ¶ Topic: <topic>/command/fs and <common_topic>/command/fs Commands are sent as JSON payloads. 1. Upload File from Remote URL ¶ action : "upload" url : HTTP source URL on the local network or internet. target : Destination file path on internal flash (e.g. "/doorbell.wav" ). Example Payload: { "action": "upload", "url": "http://192.168.1.100/sound.wav", "target": "/doorbell.wav" } 2. Delete File ¶ action : "delete" target : Path of the file to remove from flash. Example Payload: { "action": "delete", "target": "/doorbell.wav" } 3. List Stored Files ¶ action : "list" Example Payload: { "action": "list" } Publications ¶ Dedicated Status Topic The File storage module state is not included in the central <topic>/status message aggregated by the General module. File storage status is published exclusively on the dedicated <topic>/status/fs topic during/after actions, or when requested by a list command. Topic: <topic>/status/fs JSON Fields: ¶ state : Current filesystem activity: RUNNING : An action (e.g. file download) is in progress. New actions are locked until completion. IDLE : The filesystem engine is idle and ready for new requests. lastAction : The action currently or most recently executed ( upload , delete , list ). lastResult : Execution result of the last action: SUCCESS : Action completed successfully. ERROR : Action failed (e.g. download failed, insufficient space). "" : Empty string while state is RUNNING . remaining : Remaining bytes to download during an active upload ( 0 when idle). files : Array of files on flash storage with filename and size in bytes. Example Payload during upload: { "state": "RUNNING", "lastAction": "upload", "lastResult": "", "remaining": 2883800 } Example Payload upon completion or list request: { "state": "IDLE", "lastAction": "upload", "lastResult": "SUCCESS", "remaining": 0, "files": [ { "name": "doorbell.wav", "size": 2883800 } ] }

docs.text: General Module ¶ The General module provides system supervision: it aggregates status and telemetry metrics from all active modules across the device and transmits them over MQTT. Operating Behavior ¶ On startup: Automatically publishes initial device status ( status ) and telemetry ( telemetry ) payloads to the MQTT broker. Periodically: Continues publishing telemetry updates ( telemetry ) every 120 seconds . MQTT Interface ¶ Subscriptions (Commands) ¶ Topic: <topic>/command Command (Payload) Description status_update Request an immediate device status publication ( status ). telemetry_update Request an immediate telemetry publication ( telemetry ). restart Trigger a software reboot of the device. Publications ¶ Status Message ¶ Topic: <topic>/status Contains core ESP32 runtime state along with status objects from other active modules. esp.lastResetReason : Cause of the most recent reset/reboot. Possible values: POWERON SOFTWARE PANIC INT_WDT TASK_WDT WDT DEEPSLEEP BROWNOUT SDIO UNKNOWN Example Payload: { "esp": { "lastResetReason": "SOFTWARE" } // status fields from other modules are nested here } Telemetry Message ¶ Topic: <topic>/telemetry Periodically published system metrics: Field Type Description uptime integer Time elapsed since boot in milliseconds (ms). freeheap_percent integer Percentage of available heap memory remaining (0–100%). temp_internal float ESP32 internal chip temperature in Celsius (°C). Example Payload: { "uptime": 83476, "freeheap_percent": 53, "temp_internal": 34.6 // telemetry metrics from other modules are nested here } Settings ¶ The following parameters can be configured in the web interface for the General module: Device name: Friendly identifier for the device, displayed in the web UI header. Language: Web interface language (supported options: English and Hungarian ).

docs.text: MQTT Module ¶ The MQTT module manages connection and communication with the central MQTT broker, enabling remote commands, real-time status reporting, and telemetry data transmission. Operating Behavior & MQTT Interface ¶ The module monitors broker connection health and periodically sends telemetry reports detailing connection reliability. Publications ¶ Topic: <topic>/telemetry JSON Fields: name : Configured base topic of the device. mqtt_errors : Count of MQTT connection failures and disconnect events. Example Payload: { "name": "esp32_07", "mqtt_errors": 0 } Settings ¶ The following parameters are configurable via the web portal: Active: Enable or disable the MQTT client. Broker: MQTT broker IP address or hostname. Important Note on Secure SSL Connections When using validated SSL/TLS encryption, the client will not accept a raw IP address during certificate hostname verification, even if that IP is listed under alt_names in your certificate extension ( .ext ) configuration. A valid hostname is strictly required. Port: MQTT broker port (typically 1883 for unencrypted, 8883 for SSL). SSL flag: Enable encrypted TLS communication. Insecure SSL flag: Skip server certificate verification (use with caution). Base topic: Primary device topic prefix used by modules to publish status and subscribe to commands (e.g. esp32_01 ). Common base topic: Shared topic prefix for group commands. Specific modules (such as Audio and File storage) subscribe to this prefix in addition to their unique base topic (e.g. esp32 ). Client ID: Unique identifier for broker connection (e.g. Esp32_Client_01 ). Username: Broker authentication username (optional). Password: Broker authentication password (optional). Keep Alive: Keep-alive ping interval in seconds (default: 30 seconds ). Buffer size: Packet buffer allocation in bytes (default: 512 bytes , recommended: 512–1024 bytes ). Increase if using larger payloads or long topic paths. CA Certificate: Custom root certificate authority in PEM format: text -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- ... -----END CERTIFICATE-----

docs.text: RGB LED Module ¶ The RGB LED module controls addressable WS2812B / Neopixel RGB LEDs. It supports individual RGB color control and provides automatic status illumination when network connectivity fails. Operating Behavior & Offline Indication ¶ When network communication is disrupted, the LED automatically switches to predefined alert colors: Red: Wi-Fi connection failure in STA mode (local network unreachable). Yellow: MQTT broker connection failure (connected to Wi-Fi, but broker is disconnected). The brightness of the offline indicator lights can be adjusted independently via MQTT ( o_br ), ensuring the LED does not cause glare at night. MQTT Interface ¶ Subscriptions (Commands) ¶ 1. Set Offline Alert Brightness ¶ Topic: <topic>/command/rgb/rgbLed/o_br Payload: Brightness integer from 0 to 255 . Example Payload: 38 2. Set LED Color ¶ Topic: <topic>/command/rgb/rgbLed/color/<index> <index> : LED index (starting from 0 ). Payload: RGB values as comma-separated string: red,green,blue ( 0 to 255 ). Example Payload to set color: 21,5,36 Example Payload to turn off LED: 0,0,0 Publications ¶ State updates are published immediately to <topic>/status whenever: The offline brightness ( o_br ) changes. The LED color ( color ) changes. Topic: <topic>/status JSON Fields: rgbLed.o_br : Offline alert brightness level ( 0 – 255 ). rgbLed.color : Current active color in RGB format ( "r,g,b" ). Example Payload: { "rgbLed": { "o_br": 38, "color": "21,5,36" } }

docs.text: Rotary Encoder Module ¶ The Rotary encoder module handles decoding quadrature signals from incremental rotary encoders (knobs) and transmits rotation steps via MQTT. Operating Behavior ¶ Tracking: The driver tracks pulse transitions and accumulates rotational steps. Debounce & Batching: To avoid flooding the Wi-Fi and MQTT network with individual micro-events, rotation is batched: an MQTT message is sent only after knob rotation ceases , reporting the net relative position change. MQTT Interface ¶ Publications ¶ Topic: <topic>/rotaryencoder_<index> <index> : Encoder index (starting from 0 ). Payload: Net position change as a signed integer (positive for clockwise, negative for counter-clockwise rotation). Example Payload for 3 clicks counter-clockwise: Topic: <topic>/rotaryencoder_0 Payload: -3 Example Payload for 5 clicks clockwise: Topic: <topic>/rotaryencoder_1 Payload: 5

docs.text: RYG Status LED Module ¶ The RYG status LED module drives three discrete indicator LEDs (Red, Yellow, Green) to provide instant visual feedback on hardware state and communications (such as on the Button Box front panel). Status Indicators & Color Codes ¶ The LEDs indicate the following hardware and network conditions: LED Color Event / Condition Description Red Wi-Fi connection error Illuminates when the device is unable to connect to the configured Wi-Fi network. Yellow MQTT broker error Illuminates when Wi-Fi is connected, but connection to the MQTT broker has failed or dropped. Green MQTT message sent Flashes briefly to confirm successful transmission of an MQTT payload (e.g. keypress or encoder rotation).

docs.text: SHT40 Module ¶ The SHT40 module interfaces with the Sensirion high-precision digital temperature and relative humidity sensor via the I2C bus. Operating Behavior ¶ Measurement Cycle: The sensor performs automatic background readings every 5 seconds . Publication Behavior: Readings are not streamed continuously over MQTT after each sample. Instead, the most recent temperature and humidity values are included in the centralized <topic>/status payload during periodic status reports or when queried. MQTT Interface ¶ Publications ¶ Status Message ¶ Topic: <topic>/status JSON Fields: sht40.temperature : Temperature in degrees Celsius (°C). sht40.humidity : Relative humidity percentage (%RH). Example Payload: { "sht40": { "temperature": 23.62478, "humidity": 53.9012 } } Telemetry Message ¶ Topic: <topic>/telemetry JSON Fields: sht40_errors : Count of failed read attempts or I2C bus communication errors. Example Payload: { "sht40_errors": 0 }

docs.text: Time Module ¶ The Time module maintains synchronized system wall-clock time by querying Network Time Protocol (NTP) servers. Accurate real-time clock synchronization is essential for scheduled automations and multi-room audio synchronization. MQTT Interface ¶ Publications ¶ Topic: <topic>/status JSON Fields: system.unixTimestamp : Current Unix epoch timestamp in seconds. system.timeZoneOffset : Timezone offset relative to UTC in seconds (e.g. 7200 for UTC+2). Example Payload: { "system": { "unixTimestamp": 1792009053, "timeZoneOffset": 7200 } } Settings ¶ Configurable parameters in the web portal: NTP Servers: Up to 3 NTP servers can be configured (by IP address or domain name). Recommendation: It is strongly recommended to set a local network NTP server as the primary (first) server to minimize network latency. Timezone: Standard POSIX TZ string format (for example, Central European Time: CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3 ). NTP sync interval (minutes): Frequency of time synchronization queries to the NTP servers in minutes. Default: 15 minutes . For audio playback nodes, 15 minutes is recommended to maintain tight sync for timed start events. For pure sensor nodes, buttons, or controllers, 180 minutes is typically sufficient.

docs.text: WiFi Module ¶ The WiFi module manages wireless connectivity on the ESP32, providing both the setup Access Point (AP) mode and client connection to local home Wi-Fi networks (STA mode). Operating Behavior ¶ Operating Modes: AP (Access Point) Mode: Broadcasts its own Wi-Fi network ( ESP32_AP_... ) for initial onboarding and network configuration. STA (Station) Mode: Connects as a wireless client to the configured local Wi-Fi infrastructure. Important Note: AP and STA modes cannot run simultaneously . Activating AP Mode: If connection fails or credentials change, AP mode can be forced during boot using the physical button. See the step-by-step instructions in Quick start step 3 . Mesh & Extender Roaming Behavior: On multi-AP or mesh networks, the device scans and connects to the strongest signal (BSSID) available at boot, and stays connected to that specific access point until the next reboot . Settings ¶ Configurable parameters in the web portal: SSID: Local Wi-Fi network name. Password: Network WPA2/WPA3 pre-shared key.

Time Settings : 3 configurable NTP servers, POSIX timezone string, NTP sync intervals. Audio Settings : Local flash file and network stream prebuffer threshold sizes.
